Why 90% of Claude Code Users Are Missing Its Most Powerful Feature 🤦‍♂️

ZIRU

The secret isn’t better prompts or smarter models — it’s one hidden folder that completely changes how Claude works with your code

You know that feeling when you open Claude Code, type a carefully crafted prompt, and then watch it completely butcher your project’s coding style? You’re a TypeScript shop, but Claude starts writing vanilla JavaScript. Your team has a custom logger, but Claude keeps dropping console.log everywhere. You explained your folder structure five minutes ago, and Claude already forgot.

I lived in this hell for months. Every single session was Groundhog Day. I’d start by re-explaining the same project rules like I was onboarding a new hire who never takes notes. “We use Prisma here, not raw SQL.” “Put tests in __tests__/." "Zod for validation. Always."

Then I stumbled onto something that made me feel genuinely stupid for not noticing sooner.

No new plugin. No paid tier. No secret beta feature. Just a folder that’s been sitting in every Claude Code project since day one. Once I actually opened it and configured it properly, Claude transformed from “useful but amnesia-prone” into something that felt like a real teammate.

Most Developers See This Folder and Never Open It

Every Claude Code project has a .claude/ directory in the root. I'd seen it dozens of times in my file explorer. Never once thought to look inside. I assumed it was generated junk — something Claude needed internally that I shouldn't mess with.

Turns out, that assumption cost me months of wasted time.

That folder is basically Claude’s operating system for your project. Your coding rules, your custom workflows, permission boundaries, even persistent memory between sessions — it all lives there. The moment I understood what each piece does, I never had to repeat a project rule again.

Here’s the part that surprised me even more: there are actually two of these directories.

One sits inside your project. This is where team-wide settings go. You commit it to version control, and everyone on the team gets identical behavior from Claude. Same rules, same commands, same guardrails.

The other lives in your home directory at ~/.claude/. That's your personal config — things like session logs, automatic memory, and preferences that follow you no matter which repo you're working in.

Getting both of these right is what unlocks the full power.

The One File That Eliminated My Biggest Frustration

If there’s a single file you should care about, it’s CLAUDE.md. Before anything else happens in a session, Claude reads this file and treats it like gospel. Write a rule in there, and Claude follows it. Every time, without being asked.

Want Claude to run tests before committing? Put it in CLAUDE.md. Want it to use your team's error-handling pattern instead of its own default? Write it down. Want it to stay away from certain files? Say so.

Before I discovered this, my typical conversation with Claude went something like:

“Remember, strict TypeScript mode.” “Jest for testing, please.” “Don’t read the .env file." "...Why did you just use var?"

After writing about 20 lines in CLAUDE.md, every single one of those problems vanished overnight.

You can place this file in three spots. Project root for team-wide rules. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for personal preferences across all repos. Even inside subdirectories if certain folders need special treatment. Claude reads and merges all of them.

Getting the Content Right (Most People Don’t)

I’ve seen two failure modes. Some developers write nothing, so Claude guesses at everything. Others write a novel, which actually makes Claude worse — it loses focus when there’s too much to process. Stay under 200 lines.

What actually belongs in there: your build and test commands (npm run test, make build), major architecture choices ("monorepo with Turborepo"), tricky gotchas that trip up AI ("strict mode is on — unused variables throw errors"), and your team's naming and import conventions.

What doesn’t belong: anything your linter already handles, full documentation dumps, or theoretical explanations about why you made certain choices. Claude doesn’t need the “why” — it just needs the “what.”

Here’s the kind of lean, effective setup that actually works:


## Commands
npm run dev          # Start dev server
npm run test         # Run tests (Jest)
npm run lint         # ESLint + Prettier check
npm run build        # Production build## Architecture
- Express REST API, Node 20
- PostgreSQL via Prisma ORM
- All handlers live in src/handlers/
- Shared types in src/types/## Conventions
- Use zod for request validation in every handler
- Return shape is always { data, error }
- Never expose stack traces to the client
- Use the logger module, not console.log## Watch out for
- Tests use a real local DB, not mocks. Run `npm run db:test:reset` first
- Strict TypeScript: no unused imports, ever

About 20 lines. That’s all Claude needs to work like it actually belongs on your team.

Personal Overrides Without Messing Up the Team

Got a habit that only you care about? Maybe you like Claude to always show file paths in a specific format, or you want it to default to a particular test runner.

Create a CLAUDE.local.md in your project root. Claude reads it right alongside the main file, but here's the nice part — it's automatically added to .gitignore. Your personal quirks stay personal. Nobody else on the team even knows they exist.

Splitting Rules When Things Get Messy

A 20-line CLAUDE.md is great when you're starting out. But teams grow, codebases get complex, and suddenly your instruction file is 300 lines of competing rules that nobody wants to maintain.

That’s where the rules/ folder comes in. Drop markdown files into .claude/rules/ and Claude loads them automatically alongside your main config. Instead of one enormous file, you organize by topic:

.claude/rules/
├── code-style.md
├── testing.md
├── api-conventions.md
└── security.md

The API person maintains their file. The testing person maintains theirs. No one accidentally overwrites someone else’s rules.

But here’s where things get really interesting. You can scope rules to specific file paths using YAML at the top of the file:

yaml

---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
  - "src/handlers/**/*.ts"
---
# API Design Rules
- All handlers return { data, error } shape
- Use zod for request body validation
- Never expose internal error details to clients

With this setup, Claude only loads these rules when it’s touching files inside src/api/ or src/handlers/. Working on a React component? Claude doesn't even see these API rules. It keeps the context clean and focused.

Files without a paths block load every session, no matter what.

Custom Slash Commands Changed How I Work

This was my favorite discovery. If you put a markdown file inside .claude/commands/, it becomes a slash command automatically.

Name a file review.md, and you get /project:review. Name it fix-issue.md, and you get /project:fix-issue. The filename literally becomes the command.

Here’s a code review command I built:

markdown

---
description: Review the current branch diff for issues before merging
---
## Changes to Review
!`git diff --name-only main...HEAD`## Detailed Diff!`git diff main...HEAD`Review the above changes for:
1. Code quality issues
2. Security vulnerabilities
3. Missing test coverage
4. Performance concernsGive specific, actionable feedback per file.

See that ! backtick syntax? That runs actual shell commands and feeds the output straight into Claude's prompt. So when I type /project:review, Claude gets the real git diff automatically. No more copying and pasting diffs into chat manually.

Making Commands Even Smarter With Arguments

You can pass data into commands using $ARGUMENTS:

markdown

---
description: Investigate and fix a GitHub issue
argument-hint: [issue-number]
---
Look at issue #$ARGUMENTS in this repo.
!`gh issue view $ARGUMENTS`Understand the bug, trace it to the root cause, fix it, and write a
test that would have caught it.

Now typing /project:fix-issue 234 pulls up the full GitHub issue, and Claude reads it, finds the bug, and proposes a fix. A workflow that used to eat 20 minutes of context-switching now happens in seconds.

Team Commands vs. Personal Commands

Anything in .claude/commands/ ships with the repo and everyone on your team can use it. But if you have a personal workflow — like a commit message generator that matches your style — put it in ~/.claude/commands/. Those commands show up as /user:command-name and work in every project you touch.

Skills — When Claude Starts Acting on Its Own

Commands sit there waiting until you call them. Skills are fundamentally different. They monitor what you’re doing and jump in when they recognize a situation that matches their description.

Each skill gets its own folder with a SKILL.md file inside:

.claude/skills/
├── security-review/
│   ├── SKILL.md
│   └── DETAILED_GUIDE.md
└── deploy/
    ├── SKILL.md
    └── templates/
        └── release-notes.md

The YAML header describes what triggers the skill:

yaml

---
name: security-review
description: Comprehensive security audit. Use when reviewing code for
  vulnerabilities, before deployments, or when the user mentions security.
allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
Analyze the codebase for security vulnerabilities:
1. SQL injection and XSS risks
2. Exposed credentials or secrets
3. Insecure configurations
4. Authentication and authorization gapsReport findings with severity ratings and specific remediation steps.
Reference @DETAILED_GUIDE.md for our security standards.

Mention “security review” in conversation, and Claude automatically picks up this skill without you typing any command. You can also invoke it manually with /security-review if you want.

The big advantage over commands: skills can package multiple files together. That @DETAILED_GUIDE.md reference pulls in a companion document sitting right next to the skill file. Commands are standalone. Skills are bundles.

Personal skills go in ~/.claude/skills/ and travel with you across repos.

One important update: Anthropic recently merged commands and skills into a unified system. A file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and one at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create the same /deploy command. Existing command files keep working exactly as before. Skills just give you extra capabilities — companion files, automatic triggering, and frontmatter control over who invokes them.

Agents — Like Having Specialist Contractors On Call

This feature made the biggest mental shift for me. Inside .claude/agents/, you define sub-agents — basically specialist personas with their own instructions, tool access, and even model preferences.

.claude/agents/
├── code-reviewer.md
└── security-auditor.m

Here’s what a reviewer agent looks like:

yaml

---
name: code-reviewer
description: Expert code reviewer. Use PROACTIVELY when reviewing PRs,
  checking for bugs, or validating implementations before merging.
model: sonnet
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
You are a senior code reviewer with a focus on correctness
and maintainability.
When reviewing code:
- Flag bugs, not just style issues
- Suggest specific fixes, not vague improvements
- Check for edge cases and error handling gaps
- Note performance concerns only when they matter at scale

When Claude encounters a task that fits, it spins up this agent in a separate context. The agent does the deep work, condenses its findings, and sends a summary back to your main session. Your primary conversation doesn’t get bloated with thousands of tokens of intermediate analysis.

The tools field is a deliberate constraint. A security auditor should only read code — giving it write access defeats the purpose. Being explicit about permissions is part of the design.

The model field lets you assign different Claude models to different agents. Quick read-only tasks? Use the fast, cheap model. Complex reasoning? Save the heavy-hitting model for that. This alone cut my API costs noticeably without sacrificing quality on the tasks that actually matter.

Personal agents in ~/.claude/agents/ work across all your projects.

Locking Down Permissions With settings.json

The settings.json file inside .claude/ determines what Claude can do without asking, what it absolutely cannot do, and what requires your approval first.

json

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run *)",
      "Bash(git status)",
      "Bash(git diff *)",
      "Read",
      "Write",
      "Edit"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Bash(rm -rf *)",
      "Bash(curl *)",
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)"
    ]
  }
}

The $schema line gives you autocomplete and validation in VS Code or Cursor. Worth including every time.

Commands on the allow list run silently — no confirmation popup. The deny list is absolute — those commands never run, period. Everything else falls into a middle zone where Claude asks for your permission before proceeding.

That middle zone saved me more than once. I remember Claude trying to run a database migration that would have nuked my local dev data. The permission prompt popped up, I said no, and disaster was avoided. Without settings.json, it would have just run it.

Personal overrides go in .claude/settings.local.json, which is gitignored automatically — same pattern as CLAUDE.local.md.

The Global Config You Probably Don’t Know About

The ~/.claude/ folder in your home directory doesn't need daily attention, but knowing what's in there clears up a lot of confusion.

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies to every Claude Code session across every repo. Perfect for coding principles that never change — "I always want types declared before implementations" or "prefer functional style over classes."

~/.claude/projects/ is where Claude stores session transcripts and self-generated notes. As it works, Claude automatically saves things it learns — build patterns, project structure, useful commands. This knowledge persists between sessions. The /memory command lets you browse and edit what Claude has stored.

~/.claude/commands/, ~/.claude/skills/, and ~/.claude/agents/ are the global versions of their project-level counterparts. Anything here works everywhere.

Most of the time you don’t need to touch these directly. But if Claude ever seems to “remember” something you never told it, now you know where to look. And if you want a completely fresh start with a project, this is where you’d clear things out.

Everything In One View

Here’s the complete picture of how both directories fit together:

your-project/
├── CLAUDE.md                  # Team instructions (committed)
├── CLAUDE.local.md            # Your personal overrides (gitignored)
│
└── .claude/
    ├── settings.json          # Permissions + config (committed)
    ├── settings.local.json    # Personal permission overrides (gitignored)
    ├── commands/              # Custom slash commands
    │   ├── review.md          # → /project:review
    │   ├── fix-issue.md       # → /project:fix-issue
    │   └── deploy.md          # → /project:deploy
    ├── rules/                 # Modular instruction files
    │   ├── code-style.md
    │   ├── testing.md
    │   └── api-conventions.md
    ├── skills/                # Auto-invoked workflows
    │   ├── security-review/
    │   │   └── SKILL.md
    │   └── deploy/
    │       └── SKILL.md
    └── agents/                # Specialized subagent personas
        ├── code-reviewer.md
        └── security-auditor.md
~/.claude/
├── CLAUDE.md                  # Your global instructions
├── settings.json              # Your global settings
├── commands/                  # Your personal commands (all projects)
├── skills/                    # Your personal skills (all projects)
├── agents/                    # Your personal agents (all projects)
└── projects/                  # Session history + auto-memory

How to Set This Up Without Overthinking It

If you’re starting from zero, don’t try to build all of this at once. Here’s the order that worked for me.

First, run /init in Claude Code. It reads your project and generates a starter CLAUDE.md. Then trim it down to just the essentials — build commands, architecture decisions, and non-obvious gotchas.

Second, create .claude/settings.json with basic permission rules. At minimum, let Claude run your test and build scripts freely, and block it from reading .env files or running destructive shell commands.

Third, build one or two commands for the workflows you repeat most. Code review and GitHub issue investigation are the obvious starting points.

Fourth, when your CLAUDE.md starts getting crowded, break it apart into .claude/rules/ files. Use path scoping where it makes sense.

Fifth, add ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md with your personal coding preferences. These follow you everywhere and keep Claude aligned with your style across all projects.

That covers 95% of what you’ll ever need. Skills and agents are worth adding later when you find yourself doing the same complex workflow over and over.

What It All Comes Down To

The .claude/ folder is really a communication protocol between you and Claude. You're telling it who you are as a developer, what this project is about, and what boundaries to respect. The clearer that message is, the less time you waste correcting mistakes and the more time Claude spends doing genuinely useful work.

Start with CLAUDE.md. That single file gives you the biggest return on the smallest investment of time. Everything else — rules, commands, skills, agents — is optimization you layer on as your needs grow.

The developers who take 30 minutes to set this up will build faster, catch more bugs, and stop fighting their tools. The ones who skip it will keep re-explaining the same project rules every morning, wondering why their AI assistant has the memory of a goldfish.

Don’t be in the 90%.
